body: Ukrainian licence plates are long and white, with a distinctive blue and yellow strip on the left. This strip distinguishes them from Russian plates, which are fully white.

Ukraine exclusively has Generation 3 coverage, most of which was captured by a distinctive red Google car. This car is a strong clue for Ukraine as it's not found in Russia. Unlike in Russia, the car in Ukraine may have no antenna at all.

Besides the common red car, Ukraine also has coverage from a black car with a long antenna, a white car with a long antenna, and a grey car with a short antenna. These cars are not unique to Ukraine and can also be found in Russia.
Ukrainian roads are often in very poor condition, with many potholes and cracks, especially in rural areas. This can be a key differentiator from Russia, which generally has better roads.
Objects like fences and bus stops are often painted with the blue and yellow colors of the Ukrainian flag.
The Ukrainian language uses the Cyrillic script and features the unique letters Є, Ґ, І, and Ї. The presence of these letters is a strong clue for Ukraine.
The Ukrainian word for street is вулиця (vulytsya), which starts with a 'B' sound. This is different from the Russian word улица (ulitsa).
The Ukrainian word for city is місто (misto). Seeing this on a sign can confirm you're in Ukraine.
Town entry signs in Ukraine are white. This contrasts with Russia, which typically uses blue town entry signs.
Ukraine primarily uses square concrete poles, which are similar to those in other post-Soviet countries. They sometimes have white paint at the bottom.
Ukrainian utility poles often have diagonal support beams.
Wooden poles are also found in Ukraine, sometimes with concrete support blocks at the base.
Ukraine uses red chevrons with white arrows. This design is also used in Russia and Estonia.
Ukrainian pedestrian signs feature three stripes. This is not unique, as Russia, Estonia, and Lithuania use a similar design.
Guardrails and barriers are often painted with black and white stripes, a feature shared with Russia.
Large, often rundown Soviet-era apartment blocks are common in Ukrainian cities. They are similar to those in Russia but typically less maintained than in the Baltic countries.
Suburban and small-town homes are typically single-family houses, often on unpaved roads and looking rundown. They are usually made of brick with corrugated roofs and surrounded by fences.
A typical rural scene in Ukraine consists of a poor-quality road through a flat or slightly hilly landscape. Roads are often lined with trees, with open agricultural fields beyond.
Almost all coverage in Ukraine is from the summer. However, five major cities (Kyiv, Lviv, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Donetsk) have distinct autumn coverage.
Tall poplar trees are a common sight in Ukraine. While they can be found in some parts of Russia, they are much more widespread in Ukraine.
While most coverage is on main roads and in cities, you can also find ultra-rural tracks close to urban areas.
Street View coverage is concentrated on main roads and cities, with very little coverage in the southeast except for Donetsk. There is also a gap in coverage south of Odesa.
Ukrainian landline phone numbers begin with a two-digit area code specific to each oblast. A '2' as the third digit often indicates the oblast's capital city.
Modern Ukrainian licence plates have a two-letter code indicating the oblast of registration. Older plates use a numerical code for the region, similar to Russia.
Ukraine uses oblast-specific second-level internet domains, like .te.ua for Ternopil Oblast. These can be intuitive clues for region-guessing.
Five major cities have older 2011 autumn coverage: Kyiv, Lviv, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Donetsk. This coverage is mostly intact only in Donetsk and parts of Odesa.
The 2011 autumn coverage was filmed with a black car (Donetsk) or a white car (Lviv, Kyiv, Kharkiv), both with long antennas. The standard red car is not found in Donetsk.
The Carpathian Mountains in western Ukraine are very hilly or mountainous and heavily forested with curvy roads. This landscape is distinct from the rest of the country.

Forests of Baltic pines, recognizable by their tall trunks and orange-red bark, are common in the flat northern regions near Belarus. This helps distinguish them from the pine forests in the hilly Carpathians.
Southern Ukraine has a warmer, drier climate with a more arid landscape. Forests are rarer, giving way to shrubs and open fields.

Fields of blooming sunflowers are a strong clue for the far south and east of Ukraine, particularly in Kherson, Mykolaiv, and Odesa Oblasts. Unbloomed sunflower fields can be found throughout the country.
The Russian language is common in eastern and southern Ukraine. Look for Russian-specific letters like Ы and Э, or words like улица (street) and город (city).
A leaf stuck to the back of the Google car is a specific meta for roads around Ternopil, Brody, and Dubno in western Ukraine.
The older 2011 coverage in Odesa was filmed with a silver car that has a short antenna.
Around the iron mine in Kryvyi Rih, you can find red soil on dirt tracks and even Brazilian-style poles. However, the non-tropical foliage and a long car antenna confirm the location is not Brazil.
Utility poles with a red band are a unique feature of Kryvyi Rih.
A specific visual glitch in the coverage is unique to the city of Ivano-Frankivsk.
Polish-style bollards, with a red reflector that wraps all the way around, can be found in Ukraine's Zakarpattia Oblast.
The Hungarian language is common on signs near the Hungarian border due to a large Hungarian population.
Villages near the Hungarian border often feature Hungarian-style architecture, with linear settlements and single-storey houses close to the street.

Google’s special car trekker covers the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone from Ivankiv to the abandoned town of Pripyat. Roads to Pripyat mostly look normal, but inside Pripyat there are abandoned, overgrown buildings creating an eerie atmosphere.
The Google car’s antenna features a yellow flag with an Opel logo on one side of the road to Chernobyl.
